'''Ian Philip Grant''' (15 December 1930 – 1 March 2025) was a British mathematical physicist.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Grant, Prof. Ian Philip, (born 15 Dec. 1930), Professor of Mathematical Physics, University of Oxford, 1992–98, now Emeritus Professor; Tutorial Fellow in Mathematics, Pembroke College, Oxford, 1969–98, now Emeritus Fellow; Visiting Professor, Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, University of Cambridge, since 2013|url=https://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/10.1093/ww/9780199540884.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-17859|access-date=2021-01-10|website=WHO'S WHO & WHO WAS WHO|year=2007|language=en|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U17859|isbn=978-0-19-954088-4 }}</ref> He was emeritus Professor of Mathematical Physics at the University of Oxford and was elected a fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 1992.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Ian Grant {{!}} Royal Society|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/ian-grant-11526/|access-date=2021-01-10|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb}}</ref> He was a pioneer in the field of [[computational physics]] and is internationally recognised as the principal author of GRASP, the General Relativistic Atomic Structure Program.<ref name=":3" />

== Education ==
[[St Albans School, Hertfordshire]] (1939–1948). Open Scholar in Natural Science, [[Wadham College, Oxford|Wadham College Oxford]],  MA (Mathematics) (1951). Clarendon Laboratory, [[University of Oxford]], D.Phil. (1954).<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Source:<ref name=":0" />

UKAEA. Mathematical Physics Division, Aldermaston. Senior Scientific officer (1957–1962); Principal Scientific Officer (1962–1964).

Joint Research Fellowship, [[Atlas Computer Laboratory]] (Science Research Council) and [[Pembroke College, Oxford]] (1964–1969).

Tutorial Fellow in Mathematics, Pembroke College, Oxford, now emeritus Fellow. (1969–1998)

[https://www.maths.ox.ac.uk/people/ian.grant Professor of Mathematical Physics, University of Oxford], now emeritus Professor.(1992–1998)

Visiting professor, Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, University of Cambridge. (2013-)

Grant made fundamental contributions to the development of the mathematical theory on relativistic effects in atomic physics, of importance for detailed studies of all atomic systems and particularly for heavy atoms and for highly ionised atoms in laboratory and astronomical plasmas.<ref name=":1" /> He was also instrumental in the creation of computer codes<ref>{{Cite == Death ==
Grant died on 1 March 2025, aged 94.<ref>{{cite news |title=Professor Ian Philip Grant (1930 – 2025) |url=https://www.pmb.ox.ac.uk/news/professor-ian-philip-grant-1930-2025 |access-date=9 November 2026 |publisher=Pembroke College Oxford |date=7 March 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Grant; Ian Philip (1930 – 2025); mathematical physicist |url=https://catalogues.royalsociety.org/CalmView/Record.aspx?src=CalmView.Persons&id=NA4079 |website=Royal Society |access-date=9 November 2026}}</ref>
